sections.title: Front matter

summary.text: The opening of a French Bulletin article by Louis Delpy on improving cholera vaccines and assessing their efficacy, whose abstract argues that uneven protection comes from poor titration and from preparation methods based on a wrong view of how killed vaccines work. It states that protection depends on the amount of bacterial lysis products, not on counts of fixed bacteria, and proposes vaccines made from stabilized autolysates. The text then reviews natural immunity after cholera, which rarely lasts beyond six months, and stresses that antibodies detectable in vitro do not necessarily indicate protection.

sections.title: Quant

summary.text: Explains that counting vibrios in a vaccine says little about its potency, so active protection tests in laboratory animals are needed. It describes the mouse protection test and its variants by Burrows and by Sokhey and Habbu, and compares results from the two methods. The block ends by noting that oral infection of animals gives antibacterial effects in the gut that better resemble human infection.

It points out that peritoneal infection of animals differs from intestinal infection in humans, and that small producers may not test every lot.

sections.title: CONSTITUTION ET MODE D'ACTION DES VACCINS TUtS

summary.text: Explains that most killed vaccines are suspensions of bacteria fixed by heat or antiseptics, which resist lysis and give irregular immunity. It reviews lysed vaccines prepared by chemical, physical or biological means and argues that protective antigens lie inside as well as on the surface of bacteria. Evidence from other bacteria such as Pasteurella septica is used to show that autolysis products carry protective power.

sections.title: Dans

summary.text: Classifies cholera vaccines in use by culture method (agar-grown Kolle type or liquid-grown Sokhey and Habbu type) and by composition, from fixed whole cells to fully lysed products. It explains how delays and temperature before sterilization allow hidden autolysis that raises potency without changing the bacterial count. It cites Pollitzer's discussion of vaccine keeping qualities and turns to studies of autolysates against cholera.

summary.text: Reviews earlier studies showing that autolysed or lysed cholera cultures protect without losing efficacy. It recommends a simple method of preparing autolysates with thiomersal, avoiding toxicity, and adding an adjuvant.

sections.title: CONCLUSIONS ET SUGGESTIONS

summary.text: Sets out conclusions on preparing cholera vaccines through controlled bacteriolysis using strains with high autolytic power, for both solid- and liquid-medium vaccines. It also lists ways to evaluate efficacy, through serology, nitrogen or antigen assays, and animal protection tests, and proposes an international programme of work.

sections.title: SUMMARY

summary.text: The English summary notes that cholera vaccine seems to protect but lacks statistical proof, and that differing expert views may reflect uneven vaccine potency. It explains that hidden autolysis makes vaccines of equal titre differ in immunogenicity and recommends stabilized autolysates with an adjuvant.

sections.extract: Over 60 years' experience have amply demonstrated the value of cholera vaccine in protecting man against natural cholera infection, but statistical proof of its efficacy is still wanting.
